statement: Geography of the Arabian peninsula: seas on three sides, mostly desert and steppe, scarce rain, no major rivers.
Sixth-century Arabs lived in tribes, settled and nomadic; protection came from the tribe; no central state in the Hijaz.
The Byzantine Empire (Syria, Egypt) and the Sasanian Persian Empire bordered Arabia and fought repeated wars.
notes: General history; reviewer may add a standard historical reference.

statement: The Qur'an refers to the Byzantine-Persian conflict at the opening of Surah ar-Rum.
The Hijaz was not ruled by either empire or by a king; Makkah lies in a dry valley among mountains in the Hijaz.
Ibrahim's prayer on settling his offspring in an uncultivated valley by the Sacred House.
notes: English rendering is a paraphrase of meaning.

statement: Ibrahim and Ismail raised the foundations of the House.
The first House established for mankind was the one at Bakkah.
The Ka'bah made Makkah a centre of pilgrimage for the Arabs before Islam.
Quraysh held Makkah and the custodianship of the Ka'bah by the sixth century.
notes: Historically undisputed; the detailed story of Qusayy is left to the chapter on lineage.

statement: Quraysh lived by trade; the Qur'an mentions their winter and summer journeys.
Ibrahim called to the worship of Allah alone and was not of the polytheists.
The Prophet named Amr ibn Luhayy al-Khuza'i as the first to institute the sa'ibah (an idolatrous custom).
notes: Sahih Muslim 2856b on Sunnah.com names Amr ibn Amir al-Khuza'i as first to institute the sa'ibah; Muslim 2856a has the name Amr ibn Luhayy. The wording 'first to change the religion of Ismail' comes from other routes. Human review remains required.

statement: Amr ibn Luhayy first brought idols to Makkah.
notes: Narrated with attribution to the Seerah historians.

statement: There were 360 idols around the Ka'bah at the conquest of Makkah.
The Qur'an names al-Lat, al-Uzza and Manat.
The polytheists acknowledged Allah as the Creator of the heavens and the earth.
They said they worshipped others only to be brought nearer to Allah.
Pre-Islamic Arab virtues: hospitality, courage, keeping one's word, eloquence and poetry.
Inter-tribal raiding and long feuds; the weak and those without a tribe lacked protection.
Wine and gambling were widespread.
The Qur'an describes grief at the birth of a daughter and the burying alive of infant girls.
notes: The script does not claim how common the practice was.

statement: Jewish tribes lived in Yathrib and Christians in Najran.
A few Arabs rejected idols and sought the religion of Ibrahim.
Zayd ibn Amr ibn Nufayl refused to eat what was slaughtered for idols.
Asma bint Abi Bakr saw Zayd leaning against the Ka'bah saying none of Quraysh was on the religion of Ibrahim but him; he rescued girls from being buried alive.
Zayd died a few years before the revelation began.
alternatives: Commonly given as about five years before prophethood.
notes: Confirm a citable source; Ar-Raheeq may not carry this detail.
